ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Ethics review was not required for this anonymous observational survey under the statute of my institution's ethics committee, and none was sought.

According to the Masaryk University Research Ethics Committee, anonymous survey research with adults generally does not require ethics approval (https://www.muni.cz/en/about-us/organizational-structure/boards-and-committees/research-ethics-committee/ethics-review).
table.formatted: According to the <rs type="institution">Masaryk University Research Ethics Committee</rs>, anonymous survey research with adults generally does not require ethics approval (<ref type="url" target="https://www.muni.cz/en/about-us/organizational-structure/boards-and-committees/research-ethics-committee/ethics-review">https://www.muni.cz/en/about-us/organizational-structure/boards-and- committees/research-ethics-committee/ethics-review</ref>).

table.text: The aim of this study was to develop a self-report scale of AI grief in work and studies, the AI Grief Scale, and to provide initial evidence of its validity in a preregistered study in which nearly all participants were employed.

Participants came from a paid Prolific panel of UK and U.S. residents and from volunteers recruited online, and the panel was restricted to full-or part-time employment because Prolific does not allow screening participants out within a study without its in-study screening feature.

Participants gave informed consent online after an information page that described the age requirement of 18 years or older, anonymity, voluntary participation, questions about sadness, and data handling.
No names, email or IP addresses, or Prolific IDs were stored.
Decisions on H1-H4, H7, and H8 were the same in sensitivity analyses that included the two responses flagged as possible AI agents (N = 306) or only the Prolific panel (N = 302).
The findings apply to losses at work among employed adults, mostly in the UK, who were recruited through an online panel in 2026 and answered in English.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: As preregistered, I started the structural analyses at 300 valid responses, following guidance for Mokken scaling (Straat et al., 2014) and factor analysis (MacCallum et al., 1999). A sample of 300 participants gives 80% power to detect r ≥ .16 (two-sided α = .05). The panel was topped up until 300 valid responses were reached, and the data were frozen on October 23, 2026.

report: We used the LLM model 'vllm/DeepSeek-V41-Flash-1017-FP8' to check the contents of 1 paragraph that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses. Some essential information could not be detected: software ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(power_type = "sensitivity", statistical_test = "correlation", sample_size = 300, alpha_level = 0.05, power = 0.8, effect_size = 0.16, effect_size_metric = "other", software = NA_character_), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ``` ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(text = "As preregistered, I started the structural analyses at 300 valid responses, following guidance for Mokken scaling (Straat et al., 2014) and factor analysis (MacCallum et al., 1999). A sample of 300 participants gives 80% power to detect r ≥ .16 (two-sided α = .05). The panel was topped up until 300 valid responses were reached, and the data were frozen on October 23, 2026."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like: > An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group. For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like: > A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5. :::

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: AI grief at work and study: Development of a self-report scale
table.research_questions:
We will address three research questions: (1) whether the AI grief items form one dimension or a general factor with more specific components, (2) whether a short scale covering both milder and stronger experiences can be built from them, and (3) whether AI grief can be distinguished from general anxiety and depression and from attitudes towards AI.

Confirmatory hypotheses:
- H1: The AI grief items have one dominant general factor. In a bifactor model, omega hierarchical will be at least .80 and the explained common variance (ECV) at least .70. If this is not the case, we will report a general index together with subscores.
- H2: A Mokken scale with a scalability coefficient H of at least .40 and at least 10 items with item scalability Hi of at least .30 can be selected from the AI grief items.
- H3: The mean AI grief score will correlate positively with the PHQ-4, but the correlation will be lower than .60.
- H4: Respondents who report more losses in part A will report higher AI grief (Spearman's rho above .30).
- H7: AI grief will correlate positively with fear of AI (ATAI) but lower than .60, and at most weakly (|r| < .30) with acceptance of AI.

Exploratory hypotheses:
- H5: The optional scales C (lack of recognition of the loss) and D (ambivalence and complicity) will each show two factors.
- H6: Respondents who have read the essay on AI grief will report higher AI grief. Their responses will also be analysed separately.
- H8: Items describing anticipated loss (B22, B23, B33) will share variance beyond the general factor.

We will also explore the relation between AI grief and a preference for work done by people (HO1, HO2) in the same way as in H7.
table.foreknowledge_of_data_or_evidence: Authors’ limited observation of the data could not influence their analysis decisions. At least some of the data that will be used for this analysis plan has been accessed and observed by the authors. However, the authors certify that they have not sufficiently observed relevant evidence to influence their analysis decisions for this analysis plan and will not do so until after this plan is registered.
table.explanation_of_foreknowledge_and_managin: Data collection with volunteers started on 19 October 2026. By 21 October 2026, 16 responses had been collected. These responses served as a pilot of comprehensibility. We only read the open-ended comments on unclear questions and the answers to the cognitive probes, and we checked completion times. We did not compute any item statistics, scale scores, or correlations. Based on the comments, we revised several items before this registration (questionnaire version pilot-4, 21 October 2026). We randomized the order of areas in part A and made the headings of the two lists clearer, reworded item A10, reworded B18 because its original wording assumed that AI can already do the respondent's work, reworded B4, B10, B11, B21, and B23 in plainer language, added an instruction to choose "never" if a statement does not apply, and added one response option and two fields of work. The main analyses of AI grief will use the revised version. Responses to the first version will only be used for unchanged items and in sensitivity analyses. Until registration, we only monitored the number of responses by source and whether respondents completed the questionnaire.
table.study_type: Non-randomized study: Does not include random assignment of subjects to treatments or conditions. This usually includes correlational studies, observational studies, surveys, natural experiments, real-world evidence studies, regression discontinuity designs, and descriptive studies.
table.intention_for_causal_interpretation: No causal relationship inferred: This study is not intended to inform a causal relationship.
table.study_design_overview: This is a cross-sectional online survey with a single measurement and no experimental conditions. The questionnaire has two parts. The core part takes about five minutes and is completed by all respondents. It contains basic questions about the respondent (work or study status, field, frequency of generative AI use, share of work done with AI, age, gender), two checklists of areas that AI has taken away or weakened and that AI has given or strengthened (part A), 15 AI grief items with one attention check (part B), the Attitude Towards Artificial Intelligence scale (ATAI), the PHQ-4, and an optional question about unclear items. The second part takes two to three minutes and includes questions about AI use, the optional scales C and D, two items on preferring work done by people, further demographic questions, and, for people who lead others, a short checklist about their losses. Volunteers see a personal summary after the core part and can then continue. Prolific participants complete both parts in one go and see the summary at the end. The full wording of all items is given under Measured variables.
table.randomization: There is no random assignment to conditions. The order of areas in the part A checklists is randomized for each respondent ("None of these" is always last). One cognitive probe is randomly assigned to each respondent. Items in part B are presented in a fixed order.
table.data_collection_procedures:
We will recruit adults (18+) who work or study, in any field, including people who do not use AI. Respondents who answer that they neither work nor study will be thanked and the questionnaire will end. Consent is given by clicking Start after a short information page about anonymity, voluntary participation, questions about sadness, and data handling. We will not store names, e-mail addresses, or IP addresses; the country is derived from the connection. To prevent automated responses, we use Cloudflare Turnstile, a hidden honeypot field, and a minimum completion time of 90 seconds.

Volunteers will be recruited through English-language groups on social media, Reddit, and survey-exchange groups. Each channel has its own link, so that we can track the source of each response. The paid panel will be recruited via Prolific among residents of the UK and the US. Participants will receive GBP 0.70 for an estimated six minutes (GBP 7 per hour) and will return to Prolific through a completion link. We will not record Prolific IDs. At the end of the questionnaire, respondents see a short personal summary and contacts for help. We expect data collection to run from 21 October to 30 November 2026.
table.sample_size: We aim for at least 400 completed core questionnaires, of which about 300 will come from the Prolific panel. We will start the structural analyses of part B once at least 300 valid responses are available after exclusions. The optional scales will be analysed in the subsample that completed them.
table.sample_size_rationale: The sample size is based on recommendations for the main analyses. Mokken's automated item selection requires about 250 to 500 respondents when item quality is high (Straat et al., 2014), and the sample size needed for factor analysis depends on communalities and the number of items per factor (MacCallum et al., 1999). With 300 respondents, a two-sided test at alpha = .05 has 80% power to detect correlations of .16 or larger. The size of the paid panel is also limited by the budget, as the study is self-funded.
table.stopping_rule: The first 16 volunteer responses (19-21 October 2026) served as a pilot (see above). The paid panel will be released in batches and closed at 300 completed submissions. Volunteer recruitment will end on 30 November 2026. If fewer than 300 valid responses are available by then, we will extend it and report the extension.
table.manipulated_variables: There are no manipulated variables in this study.
table.measured_variables:
PART A (perceived change)
- Two checklists: what AI has taken away from or weakened in the respondent's work or studies (10 areas) and what it has given or strengthened (6 of the areas), each with the option "None of these". Areas: getting so absorbed in work that I lose track of time; the creative part of my work; the sense that my effort is worthwhile; the feeling that the result is truly mine; learning through my own effort; my ability to do my work without AI; trust that what others write to me was written by them; a clear sense of my role and what I'm good at; the recognition I receive for my work; conversations and collaboration with colleagues or classmates.

PART B (AI grief; 0 never, 1 rarely, 2 sometimes, 3 often, 4 very often; instruction: "How often has this been true for you in the past month? If a statement does not apply to you, choose never.")
- B1 I miss what my work was like before AI.
- B6 I feel sad when I think about how AI has changed my work.
- B10 Because of AI, I am less sure what my role is and what I am good at.
- B22 I feel sad about what my work is likely to lose to AI in the future.
- B21 I keep thinking about what I am losing at work because of AI.
- B3 I miss the feeling my work gave me before AI.
- B31 I'm sorry to see what is being lost from my work because of AI.
- B11 What AI is taking from my work also changes how I see myself.
- B23 I already miss parts of my work that will probably disappear because of AI.
- B4 Because of AI, my work no longer feels like my own.
- B17 Because of AI, my work feels less meaningful than before.
- B33 I feel sad that AI may soon take over some parts of my work.
- B9 I feel close to tears about what is being lost from my work because of AI.
- B32 I avoid situations that remind me of what AI is taking from my work.
- B18 It saddens me when AI does what took me years to learn.
- Attention check (8th position): "To check your attention, please select 'often'."

OPTIONAL SCALES (1 strongly disagree to 5 strongly agree)
- C, only if at least one loss was ticked in part A: C2 People around me make it clear that I have no reason to be sad about what AI is taking from my work. C9 It feels out of place to be sad about a change I also benefit from. C4 To others, my losses are just the price of progress. C10 I think my feelings about losses at work are exaggerated. C5 At work or school, there is no room to talk about what AI is taking from us. C11 Compared with people who lost their jobs to AI, I have no right to complain.
- AC, only if at least one loss was ticked in part A: AC1 It is unclear to me whether what I am losing at work because of AI will ever come back. AC3 Each new version of AI brings another loss.
- D, only for AI users: D1 AI helps me at work and at the same time takes something from me. D6 By using AI, I contribute to things disappearing from my work. D10 I hide from others how much of my work AI does. D3 When something goes well with the help of AI, the joy is incomplete. D8 I choose the convenience of AI over what I used to enjoy in my work. D4 I can't tell whether AI gives me more than it takes at work.
- AZ, a checklist for people who teach, lead, or train others (what AI has taken away from or weakened for them): their learning through their own effort; opportunities for beginners to learn my field; "None of these".
- HO1 It matters to me that what I read or use was made by a person without AI. HO2 I prefer work done by people, even if it would be faster with AI. (0 to 10)

OTHER MEASURES
- ATAI (Sindermann et al., 2021), 0 strongly disagree to 10 strongly agree: T1 I fear artificial intelligence. T2 I trust artificial intelligence. T3 Artificial intelligence will destroy humankind. T4 Artificial intelligence will benefit humankind. T5 Artificial intelligence will cause many job losses.
- PHQ-4 (Kroenke et al., 2009), last two weeks, 0 not at all, 1 several days, 2 more than half the days, 3 nearly every day: feeling nervous, anxious or on edge; not being able to stop or control worrying; little interest or pleasure in doing things; feeling down, depressed or hopeless.
- AI use: frequency, share of work done with AI, tools, and how long the respondent has used AI.
- Demographics: work or study status, field, age, gender, education, leading people, being required to use AI, having lost work because of AI.
- Other: country derived from the connection, language, link source, time spent on each page, and quality indicators (honeypot, automated browser, pasted text). From the day the essay on AI grief is published, a question on the last page of the core part (after part B) asks whether the respondent has read it.
table.indices: The AI grief score will be the mean of the answered part B items, provided that at least half of the items are answered. After item selection, the short-form score will be the mean of the selected items. ATAI fear will be the mean of T1, T3, and T5, and ATAI acceptance the mean of T2 and T4 (Sindermann et al., 2021). The PHQ-4 total score ranges from 0 to 12, with anxiety (items 1-2) and depression (items 3-4) subscores. In part A, we will count the number of losses (0-10) and gains (0-6). Scores on C and D will be item means.
table.statistical_tests:
We will first describe the distribution of each item, the proportion of the lowest response (floor effects), and missing data.

To examine the dimensionality of part B, we will use parallel analysis based on polychoric correlations and exploratory graph analysis (EGAnet) with bootstrapping to assess the stability of the solution. We use both methods because they rest on different assumptions, and their agreement makes the conclusion more robust.

To select items (H2), we will use Mokken scale analysis. We will run the automated item selection procedure with a lower bound of .30 and keep the largest scale. Items with Hi below .30 or with significant violations of monotonicity will be removed, and H2 will be evaluated on the remaining items. We will also report the results for lower bounds from .35 to .50 to show how the scale behaves at stricter thresholds, and we will check invariant item ordering. If the sample allows, we will also fit a graded response model.

To test whether one general score is justified (H1, H8), we will fit a bifactor model using the Schmid-Leiman solution in the psych package (omega function). The number of group factors will follow the parallel analysis, with at least three, as the Schmid-Leiman solution requires. We will report omega hierarchical and ECV, and for H8 we will examine the group factor that contains B22, B23, and B33. Reliability will be reported as McDonald's omega total.

We will test differential item functioning with ordinal logistic regression (lordif) or Mokken analysis by group for language (only if both the Czech and the English group have at least 100 respondents), frequency of AI use (never to a few times a month vs. a few times a week or daily), share of work done with AI, and field of work where groups are large enough.

For validity, we will compute Pearson correlations of the AI grief score with the PHQ-4 (H3), ATAI fear and acceptance (H7), and the preference for work done by people, and a Spearman correlation with the number of losses in part A (H4). We will also compute the partial correlation of AI grief with the number of losses while controlling for fear of AI, and compare AI grief by job loss due to AI and by share of work done with AI.

The optional scales C and D (H5) will be examined with parallel analysis, exploratory factor analysis (minres, oblimin rotation), and omega. Items AC1 and AC3 will only be described and correlated with AI grief.

All analyses will be run on the whole sample and separately for volunteers and the Prolific panel. We will use R 4.6 with the packages psych, EGAnet, mokken, mirt, lavaan, and lordif.
table.transformations: Frequency of AI use will be dichotomized into never to a few times a month and a few times a week or daily. In the share of work done with AI, the categories "more than half" and "almost all" may be merged. Fields with fewer than 30 respondents will be combined into "other". Each area in part A will be coded 0/1. Item responses will not be transformed.
table.inference_criteria: For the confirmatory hypotheses, we will use the thresholds stated above. Correlations will be reported with 95% confidence intervals, and we will consider a correlation positive if its interval does not include zero (two-sided tests, alpha = .05). We will not correct the confirmatory tests for multiple comparisons because each tests a different claim. For differential item functioning, we will use the Holm correction within each grouping variable. Exploratory results will be labelled as such.
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
We will exclude responses that (a) fail the attention check (any answer other than "often"), (b) have a total time on the core part below one third of the median, or less than two seconds per item on the part B page, (c) give the same answer to all 15 part B items and spend less than half of the median time on that page, or (d) answer fewer than half of the part B items. Respondents who neither work nor study are not included, as the questionnaire ends for them. Submissions faster than 90 seconds and submissions that fill in the honeypot field are not stored by the server.

We will flag possible AI agents (a ticked hidden checkbox, an automated browser, or long open answers pasted without typing) and responses with signs of AI-generated open answers (identical texts, typical phrases), and we will run the analyses with and without them (Westwood, 2025). We will not remove outliers beyond these rules.
table.missing_data_handling: The AI grief score will be computed from the answered items if at least half of the items are answered; otherwise, the respondent will be excluded from analyses of part B. Item-level analyses will use pairwise polychoric correlations, and correlations with other measures will use pairwise deletion. We will report the amount of missing data for each item.
table.exploratory_analyses: Exploratory analyses will include H5, H6, and H8, differential item functioning, the graded response model, the optional scales (C, D, the checklist for people who lead others, and the preference for work done by people), a comparison of volunteers and the Prolific panel in AI grief, perceived losses, and AI use, the responses of essay readers, and the areas most often marked as losses and gains in part A.
table.additional_comments:
The candidate items were selected from a bank of 84 items based on theory, personal accounts, and an essay on AI grief. The bank was translated and back-translated between Czech and English. Before data collection, we used a semantic analysis, ratings and item sorting by two language-model judges and further models, and a pretest with 12 simulated personas and synthetic responses to reduce the number of items. These steps served only to pre-select items and are not evidence of validity.

We will publish an anonymous dataset with numerical answers under a CC BY 4.0 license (GitHub with a Zenodo DOI), together with a codebook, the consent text, and this preregistration. Open-ended answers will not be published or quoted; they will be kept by the researcher and deleted after the analysis. Before publication, we will make sure that no combination of country, age, gender, field, and education describes fewer than five people.

The study is self-funded. A confirmatory factor analysis on an independent sample is planned as a separate study and is not part of this preregistration. Any deviations from this plan will be reported and explained in the publications.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p < .05", "p < .05", "p < .05", 
"p < .05", "p ≥ .05", "p < .05"), Text = c("‡ Differential item functioning flagged in at least one comparison (Holm-corrected p < .05 and McFadden ΔR² ≥ .02).", 
"Items were flagged by the preregistered criterion (Holm-corrected p < .05) and, more strictly, when the change in McFadden's pseudo-R² (ΔR²) was also at least .02 (not preregistered).", 
"By the preregistered criterion (Holm-corrected p < .05), the two items on sadness about future losses (Items 4 and 12) were flagged in every comparison by AI use.", 
"Only items with Holm-corrected p < .05 are listed; all other item-by-grouping tests had Holm-corrected p ≥ .05.", 
"Only items with Holm-corrected p < .05 are listed; all other item-by-grouping tests had Holm-corrected p ≥ .05.", 
"Within each facet defined before data collection, the item with the highest mean information in the graded response model was selected among items not flagged for DIF by both criteria (Holm-corrected p < .05 and ΔR² ≥ .02) and without local dependence with already selected items (Q3* > .20; Christensen et al., 2017)."
)), row.names = c(NA, -6L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .402", "p ≥ .05"), Sentence = c("Scores did not differ by share of work done with AI (more than half and almost all merged), χ²(3) = 2.93, p = .402.", "Only items with Holm-corrected p < .05 are listed; all other item-by-grouping tests had Holm-corrected p ≥ .05." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 82 columns across 1 data file.
#### Careless Responding

59 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, **17 were flagged *only* by short-scale straightlining** (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.
These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

**What this does not cover.** Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

Participants came from a paid Prolific panel of UK and U.S. residents and from volunteers recruited online, and the panel was restricted to full-or part-time employment because Prolific does not allow screening participants out within a study without its in-study screening feature.

Participants gave informed consent online after an information page that described the age requirement of 18 years or older, anonymity, voluntary participation, questions about sadness, and data handling.
No names, email or IP addresses, or Prolific IDs were stored.
Decisions on H1-H4, H7, and H8 were the same in sensitivity analyses that included the two responses flagged as possible AI agents (N = 306) or only the Prolific panel (N = 302).
The findings apply to losses at work among employed adults, mostly in the UK, who were recruited through an online panel in 2026 and answered in English.

info.title: AI Grief at Work: Development and Initial Validation of a Self-Report Scale

Faculty of Education

text.text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can take away valued parts of work, such as learning through one's own effort or the sense that a result is one's own.
I define AI grief as sadness and longing related to what generative AI takes away from people's lives and present a self-report scale of AI grief at work.
In a preregistered online survey, 304 adults, nearly all employed and mostly in the UK, rated how often they had 15 such experiences in the past month.
The items formed one strong scale with a dominant general factor, which justifies a single total score.
AI grief experiences were on average infrequent.
Scores were associated with the number of losses that participants attributed to AI and were related to, but distinguishable from, anxiety, depression, and fear of AI.
Their negative association with acceptance of AI was stronger than predicted.
The scale needs confirmation in an independent sample.

Alongside its benefits, generative artificial intelligence (AI) can take away valued parts of work, such as tasks people used to enjoy, learning through their own effort, the feeling that a result is truly their own, and trust that what colleagues send them was written by those colleagues.
Once access was removed, high school students who had practiced with unrestricted access to a chatbot performed worse than students who never had it (Bastani et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Once access was removed, high school students who had practiced with unrestricted access to a chatbot performed worse than students who never had it <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Bastani et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: People do not feel that text generated by AI for them is their own (Draxler et al., 2024), and managers who write with substantial AI assistance are seen as less trustworthy (Cardon & Coman, 2026).
text.formatted: People do not feel that text generated by AI for them is their own <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Draxler et al., 2024)</ref>, and managers who write with substantial AI assistance are seen as less trustworthy <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Cardon & Coman, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These studies document losses but not whether people grieve them.

A computing teacher has described experiencing these changes as grief (Geller, 2024), and qualitative health researchers have mapped their field's reactions to AI onto stages of grief (Sibeoni et al., 2026).
text.formatted: A computing teacher has described experiencing these changes as grief <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Geller, 2024)</ref>, and qualitative health researchers have mapped their field's reactions to AI onto stages of grief <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Sibeoni et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: However, these accounts of grief are personal or conceptual.
I define AI grief as sadness and longing related to what generative AI takes away from people's lives.
Such losses may arise in many areas of life, from personal relationships to creative activities, and the present study concerns work and studies.
The definition includes a reaction and its object.

The reaction is grief in the broad sense used for losses other than death; it includes longing for how things were, sadness, a shaken sense of who one is at work, and a loss of meaning in one's own effort.
Its object is a concrete loss that the person attributes to generative AI.

For example, a translator who now mostly edits machine translations may keep their job and income but miss finding the right words themselves, and if they feel sadness and longing about this, they experience AI grief.
AI grief also includes concrete losses that a person expects, such as a part of the work that AI will soon take over.

AI grief differs from grief supported by AI, such as the use of chatbots that simulate the deceased (Hollanek & Nowaczyk-Basińska, 2024), and from grief after the loss or alteration of an AI companion (De Freitas et al., 2026).
text.formatted: AI grief differs from grief supported by AI, such as the use of chatbots that simulate the deceased <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Hollanek & Nowaczyk-Basińska, 2024)</ref>, and from grief after the loss or alteration of an AI companion <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(De Freitas et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: It also differs from fear or anxiety about AI, which are reactions to threat, because it is sadness and longing over losses, including losses that a person expects.
AI grief is not the same as losing a job, because what is lost is often what work meant to the person.
Finally, AI grief is not a disorder but a normal reaction to loss, as is grief over other non-death losses.

Grief is not limited to bereavement, as people also grieve losses of health, work, abilities, and ways of life, which share with bereavement the loss of possibilities that gave their lives structure (Harris, 2020; Ratcliffe & Richardson, 2023). Papa and Maitoza (2013) showed that grief after job loss was distinguishable from depression and anxiety and was higher after involuntary than after voluntary loss.
text.formatted: Grief is not limited to bereavement, as people also grieve losses of health, work, abilities, and ways of life, which share with bereavement the loss of possibilities that gave their lives structure <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Harris, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Ratcliffe & Richardson, 2023)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Papa and Maitoza (2013)</ref> showed that grief after job loss was distinguishable from depression and anxiety and was higher after involuntary than after voluntary loss.

text.text: Scales of grief over job loss, impending job loss, and health loss have adapted items on longing, preoccupation, identity, and meaning from measures of complicated grief (van Eersel et al., 2019 (van Eersel et al., , 2024 (van Eersel et al., , 2026)).
text.formatted: Scales of grief over job loss, impending job loss, and health loss have adapted items on longing, preoccupation, identity, and meaning from measures of complicated grief <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(van Eersel et al., 2019</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(van Eersel et al., , 2024</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(van Eersel et al., , 2026))</ref>.

text.text: The loss of a work-related identity has also been modeled with concepts from grief research (Conroy & O'Leary-Kelly, 2014).
text.formatted: The loss of a work-related identity has also been modeled with concepts from grief research <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Conroy & O'Leary-Kelly, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Grief related to large-scale change has been described for the environment, where ecological grief concerns experienced or anticipated losses in the natural world (Cunsolo & Ellis, 2018).
text.formatted: Grief related to large-scale change has been described for the environment, where ecological grief concerns experienced or anticipated losses in the natural world <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Cunsolo & Ellis, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Similar reactions have been reported for digital environments, where users of social media platforms that had changed for the worse reported solastalgia, a sense of loss about a place they still inhabit (Cipriani, Menicucci, & Grassini, 2026).
text.formatted: Similar reactions have been reported for digital environments, where users of social media platforms that had changed for the worse reported solastalgia, a sense of loss about a place they still inhabit <ref type="bibr">(Cipriani, Menicucci, & Grassini, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Four features may make AI grief distinctive.
First, the grief can be disenfranchised (Doka, 1989), which means that the loss is not openly acknowledged, for example because others see AI as progress or note that the person uses AI too.
text.formatted: First, the grief can be disenfranchised <ref type="bibr">(Doka, 1989)</ref>, which means that the loss is not openly acknowledged, for example because others see AI as progress or note that the person uses AI too.

text.text: Second, the loss is often ambiguous (Boss, 1999), because it can be unclear what exactly is gone, whether it will return, and whether the next version of AI will take more.
text.formatted: Second, the loss is often ambiguous <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Boss, 1999)</ref>, because it can be unclear what exactly is gone, whether it will return, and whether the next version of AI will take more.

text.text: Such unacknowledged and ambiguous losses can be harder to work through because they lack social recognition and clear boundaries (Boss, 1999; Doka, 1989).
text.formatted: Such unacknowledged and ambiguous losses can be harder to work through because they lack social recognition and clear boundaries <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Boss, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Doka, 1989)</ref>.

text.text: Third, because AI keeps changing, people can expect to lose further parts of their work, so the grief is partly anticipatory.
Fourth, the loss can come together with gains, so a person can grieve and benefit at the same time.

Drawing on this literature and on measures of prolonged grief (Prigerson et al., 2021), I specified seven facets of AI grief before data collection, namely longing, sadness, identity, meaning, preoccupation with the loss, anticipatory grief, and avoidance.
text.formatted: Drawing on this literature and on measures of prolonged grief <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Prigerson et al., 2021)</ref>, I specified seven facets of AI grief before data collection, namely longing, sadness, identity, meaning, preoccupation with the loss, anticipatory grief, and avoidance.

text.text: Stages of grief, which Sibeoni et al. (2026) applied to reactions to AI, were not used because stage models lack sound empirical support (Stroebe et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Stages of grief, which <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Sibeoni et al. (2026)</ref> applied to reactions to AI, were not used because stage models lack sound empirical support <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Stroebe et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Existing measures related to AI capture threats, evaluations, or self-conscious emotions.

They assess anxiety about AI (Wang & Wang, 2022), fear of generative AI (Corradi et al., 2026), threat to work identity (Mirbabaie et al., 2022), attitudes toward AI (Sindermann et al., 2021), and shame and guilt about using AI (Cipriani, Menicucci, Greco, & Grassini, 2026).
text.formatted: They assess anxiety about AI <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Wang & Wang, 2022)</ref>, fear of generative AI <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Corradi et al., 2026)</ref>, threat to work identity <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Mirbabaie et al., 2022)</ref>, attitudes toward AI <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Sindermann et al., 2021)</ref>, and shame and guilt about using AI <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Cipriani, Menicucci, Greco, & Grassini, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Measures of job insecurity similarly concern the possibility of losing the job itself (Vander Elst et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Measures of job insecurity similarly concern the possibility of losing the job itself <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Vander Elst et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: None of them asks about grief over losses, which may occur whether or not the job is at risk and together with acceptance of AI and its benefits.
Because grief after job loss has correlated strongly with anxiety and depression (van Eersel et al., 2019), a measure of AI grief should be distinguishable from general distress.
text.formatted: Because grief after job loss has correlated strongly with anxiety and depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(van Eersel et al., 2019)</ref>, a measure of AI grief should be distinguishable from general distress.

text.text: It should also be distinguishable from attitudes toward AI, because a person can value AI and still grieve what it has taken.
Finally, the measure should be related to losses that people actually perceive.

The aim of this study was to develop a self-report scale of AI grief in work and studies, the AI Grief Scale, and to provide initial evidence of its validity in a preregistered study in which nearly all participants were employed.
In an online survey, I tested 15 items together with measures of perceived losses and gains, distress, and attitudes toward AI.
The study addressed three research questions, the first of which was whether the AI grief items form one dimension or a general factor with more specific components.

The second was whether a short scale covering both milder and stronger experiences can be built from the items, and the third was whether AI grief can be distinguished from anxiety and depression and from attitudes toward AI.
Because the scale should measure AI grief equally well in people who use AI a lot, a little, or not at all, I also examined whether the items function differently across levels of AI use.
The confirmatory hypotheses were that the items share one dominant general factor (H1) and form a Mokken scale (H2).

AI grief was expected to correlate positively with anxiety and depression, but not so strongly as to suggest the same construct (H3), and people who perceive more losses were expected to report more AI grief (H4).
AI grief was expected to correlate positively, but not too strongly, with fear of AI and at most weakly with acceptance of AI (H7).

The exploratory hypotheses were that two optional short scales outside the AI Grief Scale, one on unrecognized loss and one on ambivalence, each have two factors (H5) and that anticipatory grief has variance of its own beyond the general factor (H8).
I conducted a preregistered cross-sectional online survey of a nonprobability sample of adults who work or study, including those who do not use AI.

Participants came from a paid Prolific panel of UK and U.S. residents and from volunteers recruited online, and the panel was restricted to full-or part-time employment because Prolific does not allow screening participants out within a study without its in-study screening feature.
Panel members took part on October 22-23, 2026, and received £0.67 or £0.70, which corresponds to about £6 per hour.
The study was advertised as a survey on what AI gives to and takes from people's work or studies, without mentioning grief, and all responses were in English.

Participants gave informed consent online after an information page that described the age requirement of 18 years or older, anonymity, voluntary participation, questions about sadness, and data handling.
No names, email or IP addresses, or Prolific IDs were stored.
The core part of the questionnaire had a fixed order, starting with background questions, followed by perceived losses and gains, the AI grief items, attitudes toward AI, and distress.

A personal summary shown at the end of the questionnaire (to the two volunteers already after the core measures) introduced the term AI grief, suggested ways of coping, pointed to a directory of helplines, and recommended professional help when scores on the Patient Health Questionnaire-4 (PHQ-4) were elevated (total ≥ 6 or a subscore ≥ 3; Kroenke et al., 2009).
text.formatted: A personal summary shown at the end of the questionnaire (to the two volunteers already after the core measures) introduced the term AI grief, suggested ways of coping, pointed to a directory of helplines, and recommended professional help when scores on the Patient Health Questionnaire-4 (PHQ-4) were elevated (total ≥ 6 or a subscore ≥ 3; <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Kroenke et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Ethics review was not required for this anonymous observational survey under the statute of my institution's ethics committee, and none was sought.
The preregistered exclusion criteria were a failed attention check, implausibly fast or uniform responding, too few answered items, and neither working nor studying.

Because AI agents can pass attention checks (Westwood, 2025), responses with signs of AI agents were excluded from the main analyses and kept for sensitivity analyses (rules and counts in Supplement, Section 1).
text.formatted: Because AI agents can pass attention checks <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Westwood, 2025)</ref>, responses with signs of AI agents were excluded from the main analyses and kept for sensitivity analyses (rules and counts in Supplement, Section 1).

text.text: Of 326 submissions to the final questionnaire, 20 were excluded by the preregistered criteria and 2 others were flagged as possible AI agents, which left 304 participants.
Of these, 54% were women, most were aged 25-44 (age was collected in bands), and 91% were in the UK according to their connection.
Two thirds used generative AI for work or study at least a few times a week, and 11% were studying, all but two alongside work (Table 1).

text.text: Items are rated for the past 2 weeks from 0 (not at all) to 3 (nearly every day), so the total score ranges from 0 to 12 and each subscore from 0 to 6.

The Attitude Towards Artificial Intelligence scale (ATAI; Sindermann et al., 2021) measures fear of AI with three items (e.g., "I fear artificial intelligence") and acceptance of AI with two items (e.g., "I trust artificial intelligence"), rated from 0 (strongly disagree) to 10 (strongly agree).

These scales and items were rated from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).
Participants who teach or lead others also marked what AI had weakened for the people they teach or lead.

Its correlation with acceptance of AI exceeded the predicted |r| < .30 by its point estimate, r = -.34, 95% CI [-.44, -.24], although the interval included absolute values below .30.
text.formatted: Its correlation with acceptance of AI exceeded the predicted |r| < .30 by its point estimate, r = -.34, 95% CI [-.44, -.24], although the interval included absolute values below .30.

text.text: In preregistered exploratory analyses, AI grief also correlated positively with preferring work done by people.
Note.
Correlations of the AI grief score with other variables.
Confidence intervals for Spearman correlations follow Bonett and Wright (2000).
text.formatted: Confidence intervals for Spearman correlations follow <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Bonett and Wright (2000)</ref>.

text.text: Corrected for unreliability (omega total of both scales), the correlation with the PHQ-4 total was .36 (not preregistered; specified before the analysis).

Items on preferring work done by people and on the nature of the loss were rated from 0 (strongly disagree) to 10 (strongly agree) and from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree), respectively; the latter were answered by a subgroup.
By its preregistered wording, exploratory H5 was supported, because parallel analysis suggested two factors in each optional scale.
By the criterion specified before the analysis, it was not supported, because items did not load on their expected factors and the second factor was defined by a single item.
In the scale on unrecognized loss, this item had a loading of 1.00, close to a Heywood case (Supplemental Table S6).
text.formatted: In the scale on unrecognized loss, this item had a loading of 1.00, close to a Heywood case (Supplemental Table <ref type="table">S6</ref>).

text.text: Of the 158 participants who teach or lead others, 70.9% marked that AI had weakened learning through one's own effort among those they teach or lead, and 39.9% marked that it had weakened opportunities for beginners to learn the field (preregistered exploratory).
Decisions on H1-H4, H7, and H8 did not change in the sensitivity analyses (Table 3).
text.formatted: Decisions on H1-H4, H7, and H8 did not change in the sensitivity analyses (Table <ref type="table">3</ref>).

text.text: In checks that were not preregistered, H4 was still supported without the three areas of loss that overlap in content with items, ρ = .42.
H1 and H2 were still supported among the 258 participants who marked at least one loss (ω h = .85, ECV = .77, H = .61).
After the confirmatory analyses, I selected one item per facet by item information, DIF, and local dependence (K. B. Christensen et al., 2017; Smith et al., 2000).
text.formatted: After the confirmatory analyses, I selected one item per facet by item information, DIF, and local dependence (K. B. <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Christensen et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Smith et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: This exploratory 7-item version had a marginal reliability of .90, compared with .94 for the full scale, and its correlations with other variables differed by at most .04 (Supplement, Section 4).
The present study developed a self-report measure of AI grief at work and evaluated it in a preregistered study of 304 adults, nearly all of them employed.
Four of the five confirmatory hypotheses were supported.
However, H7 was not supported because, although AI grief correlated with fear of AI as predicted, its correlation with acceptance of AI exceeded the predicted bound.
The preregistered item selection retained all 15 items, so it did not produce a shorter scale, and the second research question remains open.
Exploratory H8 was not supported, and H5 was not supported by the criterion specified before the analysis.
Because error rates were not controlled across the exploratory analyses, their results should be treated as hypotheses.
Items covering all seven facets of AI grief measured one dominant dimension, so a total score summarizes them well.
The group factors added little reliable variance.
Contrary to H8, the three anticipatory grief items did not form a separate component, although the two items on sadness about future losses were endorsed most often.
This suggests, although it does not show, that grief over expected losses is part of the same experience as grief over losses that have already occurred (Cunsolo & Ellis, 2018).
text.formatted: This suggests, although it does not show, that grief over expected losses is part of the same experience as grief over losses that have already occurred <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Cunsolo & Ellis, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: AI grief experiences were on average infrequent in this sample, although this level does not indicate how common AI grief is, because the sample was not representative.
Scores were associated with the number of perceived losses, even when fear of AI was controlled, and were higher among participants who had lost part of their work.
More AI grief was also reported by participants who were unsure whether what they were losing would come back and by those who felt that each new version of AI brought another loss.
These two items fit the idea of ambiguous loss, in which it is unclear what is gone and whether it will return (Boss, 1999), although single items cannot show that AI grief is a form of it.
text.formatted: These two items fit the idea of ambiguous loss, in which it is unclear what is gone and whether it will return <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Boss, 1999)</ref>, although single items cannot show that AI grief is a form of it.

text.text: AI grief was related to anxiety and depression, with correlations of .32 and .33, but was distinguishable from them.
Grief before an impending job loss correlated .44 and .37 with these symptoms (van Eersel et al., 2024), and grief after job loss correlated. 63 and .71 (van Eersel et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Grief before an impending job loss correlated .44 and .37 with these symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(van Eersel et al., 2024)</ref>, and grief after job loss correlated. <ref type="bibr">63 and .71 (van Eersel et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: These studies, however, used other instruments and concerned other losses.

The structure of the scale was similar to that of scales of grief over job loss and health loss, which fitted one factor after correlated residuals were allowed (van Eersel et al., 2019 (van Eersel et al., , 2024 (van Eersel et al., , 2026)).
text.formatted: The structure of the scale was similar to that of scales of grief over job loss and health loss, which fitted one factor after correlated residuals were allowed <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(van Eersel et al., 2019</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(van Eersel et al., , 2024</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(van Eersel et al., , 2026))</ref>.

text.text: Like these scales, the AI grief items had one dominant factor with small content clusters, which may explain the poor fit of the graded response model.
AI grief was also associated with attitudes toward AI.
Its correlation with fear of AI was within the predicted range, and its negative correlation with acceptance of AI was moderate.
Grieving what AI takes may lower acceptance of AI, low acceptance may make losses more visible, or both may reflect a broader negative view of AI, and cross-sectional data cannot tell these apart.
Participants who reported more gains reported only slightly less AI grief, and the creative part of work was the area most often marked as gained but was also often marked as lost.
The loss measured by the AI Grief Scale can be ongoing and partly anticipated.

Whether it also goes unrecognized by others, as theorized for disenfranchised and non-death losses (Doka, 1989; Harris, 2020), remains open, because the short scale on unrecognized loss had low reliability.
text.formatted: Whether it also goes unrecognized by others, as theorized for disenfranchised and non-death losses <ref type="bibr">(Doka, 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Harris, 2020)</ref>, remains open, because the short scale on unrecognized loss had low reliability.

text.text: The scale can be used to study who grieves what AI takes from work and, once its stability and sensitivity to change are established, to evaluate support in counseling and psychotherapy or in the workplace.
The areas most often marked as lost, such as learning through one's own effort and the feeling that a result is truly one's own, suggest topics for such support.
In this sample, these experiences were on average infrequent, so a grief frame may be relevant mainly to people who report them often, not to everyone whose work AI changes.
The total score should be used without subscores, and the scale is not a diagnostic measure.
The exploratory 7-item version, with one item per facet, kept most of the precision and associations of the full scale and may be useful when questionnaire length matters.
Nevertheless, because it was selected and evaluated in the same sample, I recommend the 15-item scale until the 7-item version is confirmed in an independent sample.

First, the structure, item selection, and validity were evaluated in one cross-sectional sample, so confirmatory factor analysis in an independent sample, test-retest reliability, and external criteria such as functioning or help seeking are still missing.
Discriminant validity was examined only against distress and attitudes toward AI, not against job insecurity, AI anxiety, or an established grief scale.
Because every item attributes a loss to AI, the score may also partly reflect a negative view of what AI does to one's work.

Second, content validity rests on items developed with language-model assistance and on a clarity pilot with 16 volunteers, without concept elicitation in the target population, an expert panel, or cognitive interviews (Terwee et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Second, content validity rests on items developed with language-model assistance and on a clarity pilot with 16 volunteers, without concept elicitation in the target population, an expert panel, or cognitive interviews <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Terwee et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Third, although the preregistered population was adults who work or study, the panel was restricted to employed people, so nearly all students also worked.
Fourth, all measures were self-reports, which may have inflated the associations (Podsakoff et al., 2003).
text.formatted: Fourth, all measures were self-reports, which may have inflated the associations <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Podsakoff et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Perceived losses were always reported before the AI grief items, and three areas of loss overlap in content with three items.
Both the fixed order and this overlap may have inflated the association tested by H4, although a sensitivity check without these areas led to the same conclusion.
Fifth, the answer never also meant that a statement did not apply, so many responses were zero, which may inflate indices of a dominant factor.
Among participants who marked at least one loss, however, H1 and H2 were still supported.
Sixth, the graded response model did not fit adequately, so its estimates of measurement precision are approximate.
The groups tested for DIF were small, so small DIF may have gone undetected.
Items 4, 8, and 12 functioned differently by share of work done with AI, so total scores may not be fully comparable across these groups.
Finally, the thresholds for H3, H4, and H7 were set in advance but are arbitrary.
The findings apply to losses at work among employed adults, mostly in the UK, who were recruited through an online panel in 2026 and answered in English.

It is not yet known whether they generalize to students, people without work, other languages and countries, or later stages of AI adoption (Simons et al., 2017), and AI grief in other areas of life, such as personal relationships, remains to be measured.
text.formatted: It is not yet known whether they generalize to students, people without work, other languages and countries, or later stages of AI adoption <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Simons et al., 2017)</ref>, and AI grief in other areas of life, such as personal relationships, remains to be measured.

text.text: A planned preregistered second study will test the structure with confirmatory factor analysis in an independent sample, add test-retest reliability and measurement invariance across AI use and language, include students, and test the 7-item version against criteria set in advance.
The short scales on unrecognized loss and on ambivalence need revision before further use.
The AI Grief Scale gives a single score for how often people experience grief over what AI takes from their work.
In this sample, these experiences were moderately related to distress and fear of AI and were more frequent among people who attributed more losses to AI.
Before the scale is used to evaluate support, its structure and the 7-item version need confirmation in an independent sample.

These comments and a comment on unclear questions at the end of the core part were used to flag possible AI agents and are not shared.
